items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He taught a lot of people. Dexter Gordon and Eric Dolphy are the famous ones.

ctx.x: Who were your instructors? Who was on the faculty there?

Nobody famous. We had Kenny Farrar. He was one of the arranging teachers. And David Baskerville, who later became head of the program at Denver University, I think, or Colorado University at Denver maybe. Kenny Farrar is still around. He was a drummer, and he wrote arrangements, the first drummer I knew that did that. Anyway, just showing me the basics, and right away I started writing charts. Everybody thought I was some kind of whiz, because I could put down a lot of the stuff that I had heard. And I started…

through every – to a tune, every bar, going through the whole 32 bars to a tune playing arpeggios of the harmony. I got that – was able to do that, although I could have used a little more philosophy, I think. But that was not forthcoming. So I made due with what I got. It turned out to be a good thing, because a few months later I auditioned for a band here that had made some records which I had heard on the radio. His name was Ike Carpenter. On the records, he‟d use Lucky Thompson, who had a chordal approach…

items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: Then let’s see, Dexter Gordon, after I got out of the service I heard a lot of Dexter

ctx.x: Well let’s see. After Barnet I joined Kenton’s band and I was writing for him but I wasn’t writing very much. For the first nine months or so I couldn’t figure out what to write for the band, so I was making more money as a player then. Then after I left him I came back to L.A. and I guess at first I was doing more playing than writing. And then gradually, after a couple of years I think, more writing.
Who did you like — did you have some influences as far as jazz players that you tried to emulate?
